hits.text:
GPT-6.1 Terra: delivering fast and capable computer use at a lower price.

GPT-6.1 Terra understands what’s on screen, takes action across apps, writes naturally, and is a more capable model for your whole workday with the efficiency to take on more of it. https://t.co/8JTN1yonmV
hits.original:
GPT-6.1 Terra: delivering fast and capable computer use at a lower price.

GPT-6.1 Terra understands what’s on screen, takes action across apps, writes naturally, and is a more capable model for your whole workday with the efficiency to take on more of it. https://t.co/8JTN1yonmV
hits.draft_en:
GPT-6.1 Terra's whole pitch is computer use at a lower price.

Cheaper clicking doesn't fix a bad process. It just lets you run the bad process more often.

Before you point any computer use agent at a legacy app:

1. Write down the steps a human does today, in order
2. Mark every step that already has an API or connector
3. Hand only the leftovers to computer use

Connectors first. Screens last.
hits.video_tip: 30s screen record: a sticky-note list of a real process, highlight the connector steps green and the leftovers yellow, then show a Copilot Studio agent handling only the yellow ones. End card: 'Connectors first. Screens last.'

That's the bit worth telling your CIO. Picking a model isn't a procurement project anymore. It's a dropdown.

hits.hook: Generating code is easy, trusting it is the hard part
hits.text:
Generating code is getting easier. Knowing whether to trust it is the hard part.
 
Microsoft engineers share how they combine agents, testing, and formal verification to validate changes across massive codebases, including C/C++ to Rust migrations.
https://t.co/0PMocL1Onf
hits.original:
Generating code is getting easier. Knowing whether to trust it is the hard part.
 
Microsoft engineers share how they combine agents, testing, and formal verification to validate changes across massive codebases, including C/C++ to Rust migrations.
https://t.co/0PMocL1Onf
hits.draft_en:
Microsoft's dev team nailed it: writing code with AI keeps getting easier. Trusting what comes out is the hard bit.

Agents are no different. A Copilot Studio agent that answers fast and wrong is just a confident intern with tenant access.

My checklist before anything ships:

- A test set of real questions with known answers
- Knowledge sources trimmed to what it actually needs
- Activity reviewed every week, not when someone complains

Speed is cheap now. Trust is the job.
hits.video_tip: Talking head, 20s, one take. Cut to a spreadsheet test set with a pass/fail column filling in, then the agent's Activity tab. Overlay: 'Speed is cheap. Trust is the job.'

'computer use' + 'lower price' is the phrase of the day; every Terra post leads with it
AI-for-science awe, then a six-word joke from the same author (gdb 2.29M then 491K for 'p still probably doesn't equal np')
trust and verification over speed (msdev 21K 'knowing whether to trust it is the hard part', Pocock 658K on a strictly verified agent language, CodeRabbit security 47K)
leaderboard brags with a rank number (MAI-Image #2 / #3, 8.6K and 6.7K)
short personal hot takes and screen captures from devrel voices (shanselman ARM daily driver 40K, 16-bit app on ARM 6.7K)
world models are the next wave outside the watchlist (Google DeepMind Genie 4 125K in under an hour, emollick follow-ups)

drafts.text:
GPT-6.1 Terra's whole pitch is computer use at a lower price.

Cheaper clicking doesn't fix a bad process. It just lets you run the bad process more often.

Before you point any computer use agent at a legacy app:

1. Write down the steps a human does today, in order
2. Mark every step that already has an API or connector
3. Hand only the leftovers to computer use

Connectors first. Screens last.
drafts.video_tip: 30s screen record: a sticky-note list of a real process, highlight the connector steps green and the leftovers yellow, then show a Copilot Studio agent handling only the yellow ones. End card: 'Connectors first. Screens last.'

drafts.text:
Microsoft's dev team nailed it: writing code with AI keeps getting easier. Trusting what comes out is the hard bit.

Agents are no different. A Copilot Studio agent that answers fast and wrong is just a confident intern with tenant access.

My checklist before anything ships:

- A test set of real questions with known answers
- Knowledge sources trimmed to what it actually needs
- Activity reviewed every week, not when someone complains

Speed is cheap now. Trust is the job.
drafts.video_tip: Talking head, 20s, one take. Cut to a spreadsheet test set with a pass/fail column filling in, then the agent's Activity tab. Overlay: 'Speed is cheap. Trust is the job.'

drafts.text:
OpenAI shipped GPT-6.1 Terra, and the same day it was live in GitHub Copilot, VS Code and Microsoft Foundry.

That's the bit worth telling your CIO. Picking a model isn't a procurement project anymore. It's a dropdown.

So the real question: does your team have an eval that tells you if the new model is better for YOUR work?

No eval, and every launch day is just vibes.
drafts.video_tip: Vertical 25s: VS Code Copilot Chat, same prompt run twice with the model picker switched to Terra, results side by side. Caption: 'New model? Prove it on your repo.'

drafts.text:
Greg Brockman: AI helped make discoveries in math, computer science and physics.

Also Greg Brockman, a few hours later: p still probably doesn't equal np.

Me: my Power Automate flow still can't tell an empty string from a null.

We all have our frontiers.
